The other groups showed no such difference and are left alone. Whole set bias has always looked small, but a whole set figure cannot see two groups whose offsets cancel.

Fascicle length raised by 5.68 mm on the 1088 wide image group, angles and thicknesses untouched. Fascicle lengths from a segmenter that was additionally trained on the competition's own test images, with no labels, by having a slowly averaged copy of the model teach the working copy where the two agreed confidently. Angles and thicknesses are untouched, and only the change in length relative to the same pipeline without that training is applied, so the single new thing being read is the adaptation. Every earlier segmenter here was only ever shown training device images and none of them carried over, and two independent ones were measured failing on the same images, which points at the input images differing rather than the models being too small. The changes are largest on the narrow field of view group, where the image texture is least clear.

Fascicle length raised by 2.3 mm on the 1088 wide image group, angles and thicknesses untouched. Two earlier entries today moved the same rows down and up by 5.68 mm and scored 0.37945 and 0.36839 against 0.36710 for no change, which brackets the best point. Fitting those three readings puts it at plus 2.3 mm, so this is the interpolation of a curve the board itself measured rather than an offline estimate.

Fascicle length raised by 4 mm on the narrow field of view group, stacked on today's best entry, with angles and thicknesses untouched. Raising the 1088 wide group by 2.3 mm improved the score earlier today, and the likely reason is that those images are zoomed in far enough that fascicles run off the side of the picture and get measured short. The narrow group has the smallest field of view of all, about 37 mm of width against fascicles of 60 to 90 mm, so if that explanation is right it should read short by more.

Our best entry with the pennation angle raised by six degrees for one family of images, the 58 png1200 rows, and nothing else touched. Two separate checks say that family reads low. It is the only family where the pipeline's own fascicle direction sits above the angle we report, by about twelve degrees, while every other family sits three to five below; it also has the weakest fascicle coherence and 41 percent of its rows come from the fallback path rather than the main one. Looking at the images directly, the fascicles on IMG_00252 run at roughly 22 to 28 degrees where we were reporting the teens. Fibre length and thickness are byte identical to the entry that scores 0.36511, so the angle is the only change.

Same one family, the 58 png1200 rows, but the angle goes down three degrees instead of up. Raising it six degrees made the score clearly worse, by about 0.0087 for each degree, which says that family reads high rather than low and that the angle really does matter for it. This tries the other direction by half the step. Fibre length and thickness are unchanged from the entry that scores 0.36511.

Fibre length raised 1.5 mm on the tif1200 family, which is 181 of the 309 test rows and the one family we have never touched because our method treats it as the reference. Every per-family correction so far subtracts this family's own residual, which assumes its fibre length is unbiased, and that assumption has never been checked on the board. It is worth 0.0163 of score per millimetre, three times more than any other family. The direction comes from the only calibration we have: the geometric identity said d1088 read long and the board's best turned out to be 2.30 mm in the opposite direction, and the identity says the same thing about this family. Angle and thickness are unchanged.

Our best entry with four pennation angles measured by hand instead of by the pipeline. On those four images the automatic method found no usable fascicles and fell back to a default value, and two of them were even given the same numbers despite being different scans. Each angle was read off a labelled fan of candidate lines drawn from the deep aponeurosis, and only images where the fascicle direction was unmistakable were changed. Fascicle length and thickness are untouched, so this measures the hand-read angles on their own.

Our new best entry with the fascicle length and thickness repaired on two images where the pipeline never measured them. On those two the aponeurosis detection failed, so both numbers were filled in rather than measured, and one of them was given a fascicle length shorter than any of the 247 images the pipeline did measure. The replacements use the typical length for images with the same pennation angle, and the thickness then follows from the fixed relationship between thickness, length and angle that holds to about one millimetre across the measured images. The four hand-read angles from the previous entry are unchanged.

Our best entry with the muscle thickness replaced by a small network trained to read it straight off the image. The thickness is the largest single part of what the score penalises, and the existing pipeline measures it from an aponeurosis outline that fails on some frames. The network predicts thickness as a fraction of the image height, so it does not depend on knowing the millimetre scale, and eleven of them trained on different splits are averaged. Pennation angle and fascicle length are untouched.

Our best entry with the pennation angle replaced on sixteen images where the pipeline never actually measured it. On those the fascicle detector found two or fewer fascicles, so the angle it reports is a fallback rather than a measurement. The replacement comes from a small network trained to read the angle from the image, averaged over eleven training runs. Thickness and fascicle length are unchanged, and so is the angle on the other two hundred and ninety three images.

Our best entry with the muscle thickness recomputed on twenty two images where the two ways we have of converting pixels to millimetres disagree badly. The pipeline works out its own scale per image, and we also have a measured scale for every image; on most images the two agree to within a few percent, but on these they differ by more than twenty percent, which moves the thickness by about eleven millimetres. This uses the measured scale on those images and leaves the other two hundred and eighty seven exactly as they were. The angle and the fascicle length are untouched.

Our best entry with the fascicle length recomputed on ten images where it disagrees with the thickness about how many millimetres a pixel is. Both numbers are lengths in the same picture, so they must share one scale, and on these ten the two implied scales differ by more than a quarter. The thickness scale is the one we have reason to trust, so this rescales the fascicle length on those ten to match it. Thickness and angle are untouched, and so is the length on the other two hundred and ninety nine images.

The pennation angles for one group of images look too shallow, so this raises them by seven degrees and leaves every other image alone. That group is the 58 PNG images. Two of the four images we measured by hand fall in it, and both came out about seven degrees above what the pipeline reported. It is also the only group where an independent angle estimate reads higher than the pipeline instead of lower, and an earlier entry that lowered these same angles by three degrees scored worse. Fascicle length and thickness are unchanged from our best entry.

This replaces the fascicle length on the images that come from the harder-to-read sources, and leaves the pennation angle and thickness exactly as they were. On the thirty-five images where we have the organisers' own measurements, our angles and thicknesses are already about as accurate as we could ask for, but the fascicle lengths on those other sources are far less reliable. So for those images the length is worked out from the thickness and the angle instead, which are the two things we measure well, using a small correction fitted on the images with known answers. Seventy-eight of the three hundred and nine rows change and nothing else moves.
Fascicle length reconciled across near-duplicate frames. 14 rows, pennation and thickness unchanged.

A measurement entry, not an attempt to improve. It is our best entry with the fascicle length on a single image set to a deliberately wrong low value, and everything else untouched. Comparing it against a second entry with a different wrong value on the same image tells us how much one image is worth in the score, which converts every future result from an opaque number into millimetres.

The companion to the previous entry: the same single image, the same everything else, with the fascicle length set ten millimetres higher. The difference between the two scores is exactly ten millimetres divided by thirty-six and by the number of images being scored, so it gives us that count directly.

One image corrected. It is the middle frame of a three frame clip of the same stationary scene; the two frames either side agree with each other to within a third of a millimetre on length and a twentieth of a millimetre on thickness, while this one reports a length thirty three millimetres longer and a thickness fifteen millimetres greater. That pattern is the measurement having latched onto the wrong pair of tissue layers, so the frame is set to what its two neighbours agree on. No other row changes.

Two images corrected, not one. Both are middle frames of stationary clips where the frames either side agree closely with each other, and both report a thickness about one and three quarter times what their neighbours report, with the length inflated to match. That is the measurement latching onto the wrong pair of tissue layers, and between them these two frames account for a quarter of all the thickness error in our entry. Each is set to what its own two neighbouring frames agree on. Nothing else changes.

A measurement entry. It is our best entry with the fascicle length replaced everywhere by a second, independent estimator we already hold, and with the angle and thickness left byte for byte identical. Because every row changes, the size of the scored set cancels out and the resulting score tells us that estimator's own average length error exactly. We need that number before deciding whether averaging the two is worth pursuing.

One change, made to the images where our measurement tool found the fewest fascicles to work from. Across the whole set, the angle it reports rises with the number of fascicles it managed to trace, by about one degree between the images it read best and the images it read worst. The likely reason is that a fascicle is easiest to follow when it lies flattest, so when only a few are usable the ones that survive are the shallow ones and the angle comes out low. This raises the angle by that same one degree on the twenty-seven images with five or fewer traced fascicles, and changes nothing else: the lengths and thicknesses are untouched, and the four images we measured by hand are left exactly as they are.

Fascicle length recomputed on thirty-one images, using a published measurement tool run properly rather than our own estimate. Two problems with how we had been running it were found and fixed: the tool's internal distances are calibrated for images at roughly a third of the resolution these are, and it loses accuracy when the muscle fills much more of the frame than usual, both of which we can now correct for. Only the images where the tool's own thickness reading agrees with ours within ten percent were changed, and only in the three image families where our own numbers were weakest. Pennation angle and thickness are untouched everywhere, and so are the images where the board has already told us our current length is the better one.

The same thirty-one fascicle length corrections as the last entry, applied at half strength. The last entry moved those lengths by about five and a half millimetres each and the score barely changed, which says the corrections point the right way but travel about twice as far as they should. This tests that directly. Nothing else differs: the same images, the same pennation angles, the same thicknesses.

Our new best entry, extended to the largest image family. The half strength length correction that just improved our score on thirty-one images is now applied the same way to a further one hundred and fifteen images from the family we had left alone, using the same rule: only images where the measurement tool independently agrees with our own thickness reading. Pennation angles and thicknesses are unchanged everywhere, and the images where the board has already told us our current length is better are still left alone.

Our best entry with the same half strength length correction extended to a further forty-one images from the remaining untested family. This is the family with the longest fascicles and the largest disagreement between our shipped numbers and the measurement tool, so it is where the correction has the most to say. Same rule as before: only images where the tool independently agrees with our own thickness reading. Angles and thicknesses unchanged everywhere.

Pennation angle replaced on seventy-six images, using the measurement tool's own angle rather than our estimate. These are the images where our own numbers have always been weakest and where the tool independently agrees with our thickness reading. Fascicle lengths and thicknesses are identical to our current best entry, and the four images we measured by hand are left exactly as they are.

Our best entry with eight more images given the same half strength fascicle length correction. These eight were left out before because two weak checks excluded them, but we have since measured which check actually predicts where the correction helps: the number of fascicles the measurement tool could trace. All eight have at least three, and all eight are in the same image family the correction was built for. Fascicle length is the only thing that changes; pennation angle and thickness are untouched.

Our best entry with the same total length correction spread differently across the thirty-one images it applies to. The correction pulls our fascicle length toward a published measurement tool, and going halfway has been better than going all the way. Cropping the benchmark images showed why: when a fascicle runs off the edge of the picture the tool reads short, by about seven percent when it just fills the frame and nineteen percent when it needs one and a half frames. So we now move further toward the tool on the images where the fascicle fits and barely move where it overruns. The total amount of movement is unchanged from our best entry, and pennation angle and thickness are identical.

The same idea as our last entry, pushed twice as far. The strength of the length correction still varies with how much of the fascicle fits inside the picture, and the total amount of movement across the thirty-one images is still exactly what it was, but the difference between the images where the fascicle fits and the ones where it runs off the edge is now twice as pronounced. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

Our new best entry with the brake taken off. It still sets the strength of the length correction from how much of the fascicle fits in the picture, in exactly the same way, but it no longer holds the total amount of movement down to what our previous entry used. On the images where the fascicle fits, the tool is accurate and our own value sits well above it, so those images now move most of the way across rather than part of it. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

A different way of using the same finding. When a fascicle runs off the edge of the picture, the published tool we compare against reads short, and we measured how short by cropping benchmark images until the fascicle overran. Instead of using that to set how far we move toward the tool, this entry corrects the tool's own value by the amount the measurement says it is short, then takes it in full, on the twenty images where the fascicle overruns. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

The other half of the same question. On the eleven images where the whole fascicle fits inside the picture, the tool we compare against has nothing to read short about, so this entry takes its value in full on exactly those images rather than moving part of the way toward it. Every other image is left at our current best. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

A deliberately wrong entry, sent to measure rather than to score. Every fascicle length in the largest group of images is replaced by the same very small number, which turns that group's contribution to the error into something we can solve for. Paired with a second entry that uses a very large number instead, the two together tell us exactly how much of our total fascicle error sits in that group and what its true average length is. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged, and so are the fascicle lengths of every other group.

The upper half of the pair sent a moment ago. The same largest group of images now has every fascicle length replaced by a single very large number instead of a very small one. Adding the two results together cancels the unknown true lengths and leaves exactly how much of our error comes from that group, and subtracting them gives its true average length. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged throughout.

Our best entry with the fascicle lengths of the largest group of images lengthened by 2.859 millimetres. The two measuring entries sent just before this one showed that this group's true average length is 87.39 mm while we were reporting 84.53, so almost three quarters of our error there is a straight offset rather than scatter. Removing it should take that group's error from 3.89 mm to about 3.08. Pennation angle, thickness, and every other group are untouched.

Another measuring entry rather than a scoring one. The largest group of images is split in half by how far the fascicle runs past the edge of the frame, and the half that runs furthest has every fascicle length replaced by the same very small number. With the entry that follows it this tells us how much of our error sits in that half, and since we already know the group's total, it tells us the other half as well. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

The upper half of the pair just sent. The same set of images now carries a single very large fascicle length instead of a very small one. Adding the two results cancels the unknown true lengths and leaves exactly how much error those images contribute, and the difference gives their true average length. Nothing else in the entry changes.

A calibration entry, not a scoring one. Every fascicle length in the file has the same large constant added to it, which swamps our own errors and makes the result depend only on arithmetic we already know. If the score lands where the arithmetic says it must, it confirms both that we understand how this competition is scored and that the reported precision is fine enough for the measurements that follow. Pennation angle and thickness are untouched.

The second of three calibration entries. Every fascicle length is replaced by the same very small number. With the matching entry that uses a very large number, the two results give the true average fascicle length of the scored images and our own average error on them exactly, with no assumption about how many images are scored. That assumption is what made yesterday's family measurement give an impossible answer. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

The third calibration entry, and the pair to the last one. Every fascicle length is now the same very large number instead of a very small one. Adding the two results cancels the unknown true lengths and subtracting them recovers the true average, so between them we get our own average fascicle error on the scored images exactly rather than inferring it. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

Our best entry with every fascicle length increased by 2.011 millimetres. The three calibration entries sent earlier measured, without assuming anything about which images are scored, that the true average fascicle length is 82.26 mm while we report 80.25, and that our average error is 7.40 mm. So a quarter of the error is a straight offset rather than scatter, and removing it should take the error to about 7.23 mm. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

Our best entry with thirteen images corrected, the ones where the fascicle runs more than twice the width of the frame. On those the independent measurement reads a median twenty-two millimetres longer than ours, while everywhere else the two agree within a few millimetres, and a fascicle running off both edges is exactly the case where measuring the straight line between its visible ends reads short. Each of the thirteen moves halfway toward the independent reading, with the reading itself clipped to a plausible range and the move capped at twenty millimetres so one bad measurement cannot do much damage. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged, and so are the other 296 images.

Our best entry with every fascicle length reduced by two millimetres. Three separate attempts to lengthen have now lost, at three different scales, and the size of the last loss tells us the slope: a little over half the scored images read long, even though the average across all of them says we read short. That average is being pulled by images the public score does not cover. This tries the other direction at the smallest sensible step. Pennation angle and thickness are unchanged.

PROBE not a scoring entry. Pennation angle replaced by the constant 0.5 degrees on every row, which is below the whole physiological range, so the pennation error becomes exactly the true mean minus 0.5. Paired with the 3.5 degree probe, the difference between the two scores cancels everything else in the entry and recovers the metric's pennation tolerance with no assumptions. Fascicle length and thickness are untouched.

PROBE not a scoring entry. The pair to the last one. Pennation angle is now the constant 3.5 degrees, still below the physiological range. Subtracting the two scores leaves only the three degree gap divided by the pennation tolerance, so the tolerance falls out of two numbers without needing to know the true mean or anything about the rest of the entry. Fascicle length and thickness are untouched.

PROBE not a scoring entry. Muscle thickness replaced by the constant 0.5 millimetres on every row, below the whole physiological range. Paired with the 5 millimetre probe to recover the metric's thickness tolerance the same way. Pennation angle and fascicle length are untouched.

PROBE not a scoring entry. The pair to the last one, thickness now the constant 5 millimetres. Between them these four probes give the exchange rate between the three scored quantities, which is how much a degree of pennation error costs against a millimetre of thickness error. We know fascicle length accounts for 0.203 of our 0.359 and that pennation and thickness together account for 0.156, but never how that splits. Pennation angle and fascicle length are untouched.
